TRUST MODIFICATION AND TERMINATION BY CONSENT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · The Jane Doe Revocable Trust

BACKGROUND INFORMATION — MODIFYING OR TERMINATING AN IRREVOCABLE TRUST BY CONSENT
This information sheet describes the statutory mechanisms California's Probate Code provides for modifying or terminating an irrevocable trust — potentially The Jane Doe Revocable Trust, executed January 1, 2015, of which John Smith serves, or has been asked to serve, as trustee — through the consent of the settlor, the beneficiaries, or both, rather than through a settlor's unilateral exercise of a reserved power. It covers two distinct statutory paths found at Probate Code §§ 15403-15404: a court-petition route available to all beneficiaries of an irrevocable trust acting together, without any need for the settlor's involvement, and a written-consent route available to a settlor and all beneficiaries acting together, without any need for court approval. It also covers two related, consent-independent statutory bases on which a court can modify or terminate a trust: unanticipated changed circumstances (§ 15409) and a trust whose value has become too low relative to administration costs (§ 15408), including a trustee's own statutory power to terminate a sufficiently small trust without going to court at all. This information sheet does not itself modify or terminate The Jane Doe Revocable Trust or any other trust, does not constitute the written consent that §§ 15403-15404 describe, does not constitute a petition to any court, and does not determine whether any specific trust, settlor, or beneficiary satisfies the requirements described in this document. This document is distinct from this corpus's Trust Amendment document, which addresses a settlor's own power under Probate Code § 15402 to amend or revoke a trust that remains revocable by that settlor alone, and from this corpus's Trust Decanting document, which addresses a trustee's power under the Uniform Trust Decanting Act to redirect trust principal without beneficiary consent at all. The mechanisms described here instead apply once a trust is no longer one a settlor can simply amend alone, or apply regardless of revocability, and in every version described here except the settlor-and-beneficiaries written-consent route, at least one beneficiary's agreement or participation is part of the statutory requirement.

TWO DISTINCT CONSENT-BASED ROUTES: ALL BENEFICIARIES TO COURT, OR SETTLOR AND ALL BENEFICIARIES WITHOUT COURT
Probate Code § 15403(a) provides that if all beneficiaries of an irrevocable trust consent, they may petition the court for modification or termination of the trust — a route open to the beneficiaries acting together, without the statute requiring the settlor's consent or participation. Separately, Probate Code § 15404(a) provides that a trust may be modified or terminated by the written consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries without court approval of the modification or termination — a route that dispenses with a court petition entirely, but only when the settlor, not just the beneficiaries, joins in written consent. These are two different statutory mechanisms with two different sets of required participants and two different procedural paths (court petition versus no court at all), not two descriptions of the same option.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (b), if all beneficiaries of an irrevocable trust consent, they may petition the court for modification or termination of the trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15403(a) (California Legislative Information text), the beneficiary-consent, court-petition route (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15403.)
  "A trust may be modified or terminated by the written consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries without court approval of the modification or termination."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15404(a) (California Legislative Information text), the settlor-and-beneficiary written-consent route, without court approval (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15404.)

This clause cites two different statutory sections, Probate Code §§ 15403(a) and 15404(a); both come from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text returned both times. This document does not determine whether any specific trust is, in fact, irrevocable, whether a specific group of people constitutes all of a specific trust's beneficiaries, or whether a specific settlor is alive, competent, and willing to join a written consent — those are fact- and instrument-specific questions this document does not resolve. THE MATERIAL-PURPOSE LIMITATION ON THE ALL-BENEFICIARIES COURT-PETITION ROUTE
The beneficiary-consent court-petition route described in Probate Code § 15403(a) is not unconditional. Under § 15403(b), if the continuance of the trust is necessary to carry out a material purpose of the trust, the trust cannot be modified or terminated even with all beneficiaries' consent unless the court, in its discretion, determines that the reason for doing so under the circumstances outweighs the interest in accomplishing that material purpose. A separate, additional limitation applies where the trust contains a valid spendthrift-type restraint on transfer of a beneficiary's interest under Probate Code §§ 15300-15309: § 15403(b) provides that such a trust may not be terminated unless the court determines there is good cause to do so, independent of the material-purpose balancing test.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]

  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15403(b) (California Legislative Information text), the material-purpose limitation on modification or termination by beneficiary consent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15403.)
  "If the trust is subject to a valid restraint on the transfer of a beneficiary’s interest as provided in Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 15300), the trust may not be terminated unless the court determines there is good cause to do so."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15403(b) (California Legislative Information text), the separate good-cause requirement for terminating a trust with a valid spendthrift-type restraint on transfer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15403.)

This document does not determine whether any specific trust provision constitutes a 'material purpose' within the meaning of § 15403(b), whether the balance the statute describes favors modification or termination in any particular case, whether a specific trust's spendthrift-type language is a 'valid restraint on the transfer of a beneficiary's interest' under Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 15300), or what would constitute 'good cause' for a court in a specific case — those are fact-, instrument-, and case-specific determinations this document does not make. A CourtListener case-law search on the material-purpose doctrine returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (125/day quota exhausted) at the time this document was researched; no California case law construing what counts as a 'material purpose' is cited in this document, though that phrase has been the subject of substantial published California case law that this document does not reach.

THE WITHOUT-COURT ROUTE REQUIRES THE SETTLOR'S OWN CONSENT, NOT ONLY THE BENEFICIARIES'
Probate Code § 15404(a)'s without-court-approval route describes the written consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries — both, not either. Section 15404(b) addresses what happens when unanimity is incomplete on that route: if any beneficiary does not consent to the modification or termination of the trust, the court may modify or partially terminate the trust upon petition to the court by the other beneficiaries, with the consent of the settlor, if the interests of the beneficiaries who do not consent are not substantially impaired. Even this partial-consent variant, in other words, is framed around the settlor's consent being present; § 15404 does not describe a version of its own procedure in which beneficiaries proceed under that section without the settlor. A settlor who has died, or who lacks the capacity to consent, is accordingly not a participant § 15404 contemplates being able to supply; § 15403's all-beneficiaries court-petition route, described in a separate clause of this document, does not have a settlor-consent requirement built into its own text.

  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15404(a) (California Legislative Information text), the written-consent, without-court route requiring both the settlor and all beneficiaries (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15404.)
  "If any beneficiary does not consent to the modification or termination of the trust, the court may modify or partially terminate the trust upon petition to the court by the other beneficiaries, with the consent of the settlor, if the interests of the beneficiaries who do not consent are not substantially impaired."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15404(b) (California Legislative Information text), the partial-consent variant, which also requires the settlor's consent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15404.)

This document does not determine whether a specific settlor is, in fact, deceased, incapacitated, or otherwise unable to consent, or whether a specific proposed modification would 'substantially impair' a non-consenting beneficiary's interests within the meaning of § 15404(b) — those are fact-specific determinations this document does not make. LIMITING WHOSE CONSENT IS NEEDED WHEN REMAINDER BENEFICIARIES ARE DESCRIBED ONLY AS 'HEIRS' OR 'NEXT OF KIN'
Both § 15403(c) and § 15404(c) address the same recurring drafting problem in identical language: where a trust provides for the disposition of principal to a class of persons described only as 'heirs' or 'next of kin' of the settlor, or using other words describing the class of all persons who would take under the rules of intestacy, obtaining every such person's consent to a modification or termination can be impractical, since the membership of that class is not fixed until the settlor's death. To address this, both sections give the court a narrowing power: the court may limit the class of beneficiaries whose consent is necessary to modify or terminate a trust to the beneficiaries who are reasonably likely to take under the circumstances. This narrowing power applies identically whether the beneficiaries are proceeding under § 15403's court-petition route or under § 15404's settlor-and-beneficiary route.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]

  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15403(c) (California Legislative Information text), the court's power to narrow the consenting class where beneficiaries are described only as heirs or next of kin (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15403.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trust-modification framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document does not determine whether a specific trust's remainder-beneficiary language in fact falls within the 'heirs' or 'next of kin' class described in §§ 15403(c) and 15404(c), or which specific persons a court would find 'reasonably likely to take under the circumstances' in a given case — those are instrument- and fact-specific determinations this document does not make, and only a court can exercise the narrowing power these sections describe. A SEPARATE, CONSENT-INDEPENDENT BASIS: CIRCUMSTANCES THE SETTLOR DID NOT KNOW ABOUT OR ANTICIPATE
Probate Code § 15409 provides a statutory basis for court modification or termination that does not depend on beneficiary or settlor consent at all. On petition by a trustee or beneficiary, the court may modify the administrative or dispositive provisions of the trust or terminate the trust if, owing to circumstances not known to the settlor and not anticipated by the settlor, the continuation of the trust under its terms would defeat or substantially impair the accomplishment of the purposes of the trust. If necessary to carry out the trust's purposes in that situation, § 15409(a) further allows the court to order the trustee to do acts that are not authorized or are forbidden by the trust instrument. Section 15409(b) directs the court to consider any restraint on transfer of a beneficiary's interest as one factor in its decision, without that restraint by itself precluding the court from modifying or terminating the trust. This is a materially different statutory basis from the consent-based routes described elsewhere in this document: it can be invoked by a single trustee or a single beneficiary through a petition, without needing any other beneficiary's or the settlor's agreement, but only on the specific and narrower showing that unanticipated circumstances are defeating or substantially impairing the trust's purposes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "On petition by a trustee or beneficiary, the court may modify the administrative or dispositive provisions of the trust or terminate the trust if, owing to circumstances not known to the settlor and not anticipated by the settlor, the continuation of the trust under its terms would defeat or substantially impair the accomplishment of the purposes of the trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15409(a) (California Legislative Information text), court modification or termination for circumstances not known to or anticipated by the settlor (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15409.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trust-modification framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document does not determine whether any specific circumstance was, in fact, unknown to or unanticipated by a specific settlor, or whether continuation of a specific trust under its existing terms would defeat or substantially impair that trust's purposes — those are fact-specific determinations only a court can make on a full record, and this document does not attempt to apply this standard to any actual trust. A CourtListener case-law search on this topic returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (125/day quota exhausted) at the time this document was researched, so no California case law applying § 15409 is cited in this document.

COURT TERMINATION, AND A TRUSTEE'S OWN POWER TO TERMINATE, A TRUST THAT HAS BECOME TOO SMALL TO JUSTIFY ITS ADMINISTRATION COSTS
Probate Code § 15408(a) provides another consent-independent basis: on petition by a trustee or beneficiary, if the court determines that the fair market value of the principal of a trust has become so low in relation to the cost of administration that continuation of the trust under its existing terms will defeat or substantially impair the accomplishment of its purposes, the court may, in its discretion and in a manner that conforms as nearly as possible to the intention of the settlor, order any of the following: termination of the trust, modification of the trust, or appointment of a new trustee. Separately, § 15408(b) gives the trustee a self-executing power that does not require a court petition at all: notwithstanding subdivision (a), if the fair market value of the principal of a trust does not exceed one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000) in value, the trustee has the power to terminate the trust. Section 15408(c) confirms that a spendthrift-type restraint on transfer of a beneficiary's interest does not by itself prevent application of this section.

  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15408(a) (California Legislative Information text), court-ordered termination, modification, or trustee replacement for a trust too small relative to administration costs (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15408.)
  "Notwithstanding subdivision (a), if the fair market value of the principal of a trust does not exceed one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000) in value, the trustee has the power to terminate the trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15408(b) (California Legislative Information text), the trustee's own power to terminate a trust with principal not exceeding $100,000, without a court petition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15408.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trust-modification framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. The $100,000 self-termination threshold in § 15408(b) reflects a 2024 amendment (effective January 1, 2025); this document does not represent that this threshold has always been $100,000 or that it will remain $100,000 going forward, and this document does not determine the fair market value of the principal of any specific trust or whether that value in fact falls at or below the statutory threshold. This document also does not determine whether a specific trust's administration costs are, in fact, disproportionate to its principal for purposes of § 15408(a)'s separate, no-dollar-threshold court-petition route. A CourtListener case-law search on this topic returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (125/day quota exhausted) at the time this document was researched, so no California case law applying § 15408 is cited in this document.

HOW TRUST PROPERTY IS DISTRIBUTED WHEN A TRUST IS TERMINATED BY CONSENT OF THE SETTLOR AND ALL BENEFICIARIES
Probate Code § 15410 addresses how trust property is disposed of once a trust terminates, and treats termination by consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries as its own distinct category, separate from termination by revocation. Under § 15410(c), in the case of a trust that is terminated by the consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries, the property is disposed of as agreed by the settlor and all beneficiaries — the statute defers to whatever distribution those parties actually agreed to as part of consenting to the termination, rather than imposing a default distribution scheme on that category the way § 15410 does for revocation (subdivisions (a) and (b)) or for other cases (subdivision (d)).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In the case of a trust that is terminated by the consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries, as agreed by the settlor and all beneficiaries."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15410(c) (California Legislative Information text), disposition of trust property on termination by consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15410.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trust-modification framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document does not determine what distribution terms any specific settlor and beneficiaries actually agreed to, or whether a specific termination in fact falls within § 15410(c)'s consent-based category rather than one of § 15410's other categories (revocation under subdivisions (a) or (b), or the residual category under subdivision (d)) — those are fact-specific determinations this document does not make. A CourtListener case-law search on this topic returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (125/day quota exhausted) at the time this document was researched, so no California case law applying § 15410 is cited in this document.

HOW THIS DOCUMENT DIFFERS FROM THIS CORPUS'S TRUST AMENDMENT AND TRUST DECANTING DOCUMENTS
This corpus's Trust Amendment document addresses a settlor's own statutory power under Probate Code § 15402 to amend a trust that remains revocable by that settlor alone, exercised by the settlor without needing any beneficiary's consent. This corpus's Trust Decanting document addresses a trustee's power under California's Uniform Trust Decanting Act (Probate Code § 19501 et seq.) to distribute principal from an existing irrevocable trust into a new trust with different terms, exercised by an authorized fiduciary without needing beneficiary consent as a precondition, subject to a notice-and-objection process. This document, by contrast, addresses modification or termination of an irrevocable trust — potentially The Jane Doe Revocable Trust — through the consent-based mechanisms of Probate Code §§ 15403-15404 (which in every version require at least one category of person's affirmative consent: all beneficiaries, or the settlor and all beneficiaries), and the related, consent-independent court mechanisms of §§ 15408-15409 (which instead require a specific statutory showing: unanticipated changed circumstances, or disproportionate administration costs). None of the mechanisms described in this document is available merely because a settlor, trustee, or beneficiary of The Jane Doe Revocable Trust would prefer different terms; each requires either the specific consent, or the specific statutory showing, that the corresponding clause of this document describes.

To address this, both sections give the court a narrowing power: the court may limit the class of beneficiaries whose consent is necessary to modify or terminate a trust to the beneficiaries who are reasonably likely to take under the circumstances. This narrowing power applies identically whether the beneficiaries are proceeding under § 15403's court-petition route or under § 15404's settlor-and-beneficiary route.

expectedJSON.body: Probate Code § 15409 provides a statutory basis for court modification or termination that does not depend on beneficiary or settlor consent at all. On petition by a trustee or beneficiary, the court may modify the administrative or dispositive provisions of the trust or terminate the trust if, owing to circumstances not known to the settlor and not anticipated by the settlor, the continuation of the trust under its terms would defeat or substantially impair the accomplishment of the purposes of the trust. If necessary to carry out the trust's purposes in that situation, § 15409(a) further allows the court to order the trustee to do acts that are not authorized or are forbidden by the trust instrument. Section 15409(b) directs the court to consider any restraint on transfer of a beneficiary's interest as one factor in its decision, without that restraint by itself precluding the court from modifying or terminating the trust. This is a materially different statutory basis from the consent-based routes described elsewhere in this document: it can be invoked by a single trustee or a single beneficiary through a petition, without needing any other beneficiary's or the settlor's agreement, but only on the specific and narrower showing that unanticipated circumstances are defeating or substantially impairing the trust's purposes.

expectedJSON.body: Probate Code § 15408(a) provides another consent-independent basis: on petition by a trustee or beneficiary, if the court determines that the fair market value of the principal of a trust has become so low in relation to the cost of administration that continuation of the trust under its existing terms will defeat or substantially impair the accomplishment of its purposes, the court may, in its discretion and in a manner that conforms as nearly as possible to the intention of the settlor, order any of the following: termination of the trust, modification of the trust, or appointment of a new trustee. Separately, § 15408(b) gives the trustee a self-executing power that does not require a court petition at all: notwithstanding subdivision (a), if the fair market value of the principal of a trust does not exceed one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000) in value, the trustee has the power to terminate the trust. Section 15408(c) confirms that a spendthrift-type restraint on transfer of a beneficiary's interest does not by itself prevent application of this section.

expectedJSON.body: Probate Code § 15410 addresses how trust property is disposed of once a trust terminates, and treats termination by consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries as its own distinct category, separate from termination by revocation. Under § 15410(c), in the case of a trust that is terminated by the consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries, the property is disposed of as agreed by the settlor and all beneficiaries — the statute defers to whatever distribution those parties actually agreed to as part of consenting to the termination, rather than imposing a default distribution scheme on that category the way § 15410 does for revocation (subdivisions (a) and (b)) or for other cases (subdivision (d)).
